claim: Tactile information available to the rat vibrissal system begins as external forces that cause whisker deformations, which in turn excite mechanoreceptors in the follicle.
source: Tactile information available to the rat vibrissal system begins as external forces that cause whisker deformations, which in turn excite mechanoreceptors in the follicle.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about mechanotransduction in the vibrissal system.

claim: Primary sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion (Vg) have often been described as encoding the kinematics (geometry) of object contact.
source: Despite the fundamental mechanical origin of tactile information, primary sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion (Vg) have often been described as encoding the kinematics (geometry) of object contact.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing literature, implicitly citing previous work.

claim: Vg neurons more directly encode mechanical signals when the whisker is deflected in a decoupled stimulus space.
source: We employed a novel manual stimulation technique to deflect whiskers in a way that decouples kinematics from mechanics, and used Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) to show that Vg neurons more directly encode mechanical signals when the whisker is deflected in this decoupled stimulus space.
evidence: This claim is supported by the GLM analysis performed on experimental data in the study.

claim: Deformations of the vibrissae are transduced by mechanoreceptors in the follicle.
source: Deformations of the vibrissae are transduced by mechanoreceptors in the follicle (Ebara et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ebara et al., 2002.

claim: The resulting electrical signals from mechanoreceptors are integrated by primary sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion (Vg).
source: Deformations of the vibrissae are transduced by mechanoreceptors in the follicle (Ebara et al., 2002), and the resulting electrical signals are integrated by primary sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion (Vg).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the vibrissal sensory pathway.

claim: From the Vg, signals are relayed to the brainstem trigeminal nuclei, thalamus, and primary somatosensory cortex.
source: From the Vg, signals are relayed to the brainstem trigeminal nuclei, thalamus, and primary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This describes the known anatomical pathway of the trigeminal system.

claim: Neurons in the Vg are the 'gatekeepers' of tactile information for the vibrissal trigeminal system.
source: Neurons in the Vg are thus the 'gatekeepers' of tactile information for the vibrissal trigeminal system (Jones et al., 2004a; Leiser and Moxon, 2006, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jones et al., 2004a and Leiser and Moxon, 2006, 2007.

claim: Rodents can use their vibrissae to localize objects with high precision.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that rodents can use their vibrissae to localize objects with high precision (Kleinfeld and Deschênes, 2011; Knutsen and Ahissar, 2009; Knutsen et al., 2006; Krupa et al., 2001; Mehta et al., 2007; O'Connor et al., 2010; Pammer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Previous work has focused on quantifying the response of Vg neurons in terms of kinematic (geometric) variables of contact, including radial distance to an object, angular position, and angular velocity.
source: Accordingly, previous work has focused on quantifying the response of Vg neurons in terms of kinematic (geometric) variables of contact, including radial distance to an object, angular position, and angular velocity (Gibson and Welker, 1983a, 1983b; Jones et al., 2004a, 2004b; Leiser and Moxon, 2007; Lichtenstein et al., 1990; Lottem and Azouz, 2009, 2011; Lottem et al., 2015; Shoykhet et al., 2000, 2003; Szwed et al., 2003, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: If Vg neurons were to encode kinematic variables, a transformation from mechanical variables at the base of the whisker into kinematic variables would have to occur within the follicle and/or through the primary afferent integration of mechanoreceptor responses.
source: If Vg neurons were to encode kinematic variables, a transformation from mechanical variables at the base of the whisker into kinematic variables would have to occur within the follicle (Whiteley et al., 2015) and/or through the primary afferent integration of mechanoreceptor responses.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be required for kinematic encoding, with a citation to Whiteley et al., 2015.

claim: The kinematics and mechanics of contact are tightly coupled under most standard experimental protocols.
source: It is challenging to disentangle these alternatives because the kinematics and mechanics of contact are tightly coupled under most standard experimental protocols
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of standard experimental protocols.

claim: The coupling between kinematics and mechanics is especially strong during small angle deflections and when deflections occur near the whisker base.
source: this coupling is especially strong during small angle deflections and when deflections occur near the whisker base.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of whisker bending.

claim: The intrinsic coupling between kinematics and mechanics and the absence of mechanical modeling have prevented a quantitative evaluation of the extent to which Vg neurons respond to kinematic vs. mechanical inputs.
source: To date, this intrinsic coupling and the absence of mechanical modeling have prevented a quantitative evaluation of the extent to which Vg neurons respond to kinematic vs. mechanical inputs.
evidence: This is an inference about limitations of previous studies.

claim: A novel manual stimulation technique was developed that allowed imposition of large angle deflections far from the whisker base.
source: In the present study, we developed a novel manual stimulation technique that allowed us to impose large angle deflections far from the whisker base
evidence: This describes a methodological development in the present study.

claim: The novel manual stimulation technique allows systematic exploration of large regions of the tactile input space in which mechanics and kinematics decouple.
source: we developed a novel manual stimulation technique that allowed us to impose large angle deflections far from the whisker base, and thereby to systematically explore large regions of the tactile input space in which mechanics and kinematics decouple.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Single Vg neurons were recorded in both anesthetized and awake animals.
source: We recorded from single Vg neurons in both anesthetized and awake animals
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The kinematics of contact were extracted from high-speed video.
source: extracted the kinematics of contact from high-speed video
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The mechanics of contact were computed using a quasi-static model of whisker bending.
source: computed the mechanics of contact using a quasi-static model of whisker bending.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) were used to quantify Vg responses in terms of both kinematic and mechanical variables.
source: We then used Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) to quantify Vg responses in terms of both sets of variables and investigate which description more accurately predicts Vg firing rate.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: Only when the input space is large and kinematics are decoupled from mechanics does mechanical information better predict firing activity for a majority of Vg neurons.
source: We found that only when the input space is large and kinematics are decoupled from mechanics does mechanical information better predict firing activity for a majority of Vg neurons.

source: We recorded high-speed video (300 fps) during manual deflection of 18 single whiskers in anesthetized rats while simultaneously recording neural responses from 22 Vg neurons.

source: We recorded high-speed video (300 fps) during manual deflection of 18 single whiskers in anesthetized rats while simultaneously recording neural responses from 22 Vg neurons.

claim: Whiskers were deflected with a hand-held graphite probe in two directions (rostro-caudal and caudo-rostral).
source: Whiskers were deflected with a hand-held graphite probe in two directions (rostro-caudal and caudo-rostral)
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Whisker deflections had amplitudes up to several mm.
source: with amplitudes up to several mm.

claim: Stimulation was delivered at variable radial distances that ranged up to ~90% of the whisker length.
source: Stimulation was delivered at variable radial distances that ranged up to ~90% of the whisker length
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters.

claim: Stimulation was delivered at two speeds: 'fast' and 'slow.'
source: and at two speeds: 'fast' and 'slow.'

claim: Manual stimulation caused radial distance of contact, velocity, and deflection amplitude to vary across deflections.
source: Note that manual stimulation caused radial distance of contact, velocity, and deflection amplitude to vary across deflections.

claim: The two dimensional (2D) whisker shape was tracked in each video frame to quantify the kinematic and mechanical variables of contact.
source: The two dimensional (2D) whisker shape was tracked in each video frame to quantify the kinematic and mechanical variables of contact.

claim: Kinematic variables consist of the radial distance of contact (r), the angular displacement (θdeflection), and the velocity of deflection (V).
source: Kinematic variables are illustrated in Figure 2A and consist of the radial distance of contact (r), the angular displacement (θdeflection), and the velocity of deflection (V, the temporal derivative of θdeflection, not shown).

claim: Kinematic variables were extracted directly from the shape of the whisker.
source: Kinematic variables were extracted directly from the shape of the whisker, as detailed in Materials and methods.

claim: During non-contact times, all kinematic variables are undefined.
source: During non-contact times, all kinematic variables are undefined.

claim: The mechanical variables of contact were computed numerically based on the full tracked whisker shape using a quasi-static, frictionless model of elastic beam bending.

claim: Because the mechanical model is quasi-static, all mechanical signals are exactly zero during periods of non-contact.
source: Because the mechanical model is quasi-static, all mechanical signals are exactly zero during periods of non-contact.

claim: Each deflection varies slightly from every other deflection, reflecting the naturalistic variability of manual stimulation.
source: Notice that each deflection varies slightly from every other deflection, reflecting the naturalistic variability of manual stimulation.

source: In a separate group of animals we recorded high-speed video (1000 fps) while rats explored a vertical pole (seven whiskers, nine neurons).

source: Although this variable is represented in Vg responses during non-contact whisking (Wallach et al., 2016)

source: and is of clear importance in central trigeminal structures (Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; Fee et al., 1997)

claim: Manual stimulation can involve large angle deflections (up to 60°) at large radial distances (up to 45 mm) more consistently than in the actively behaving animal.
source: Manual stimulation can involve large angle deflections (up to 60°) at large radial distances (up to 45 mm) more consistently than in the actively behaving animal.

claim: Exploring large regions of input space decouples the kinematic and mechanical inputs.
source: Exploring these large regions decouples the kinematic and mechanical inputs, allowing us to address the question of whether Vg neurons encode mechanics or kinematics.

source: Given that the follicle-whisker junction has been shown to be rigid in the anesthetized animal (Bagdasarian et al., 2013), blood-based hydrostatic changes are unlikely to be responsible for differences in rigidity between awake and anesthetized states.

claim: Changes in muscle activation are a potentially significant effect that remains to be fully investigated.
source: Changes in muscle activation, however, are a potentially significant effect that remains to be fully investigated.

claim: In the anesthetized animal, large translations and rotations of the follicle in the skin were observed when a force is applied to the stiff, proximal portion of the whisker.
source: In the anesthetized animal, we observed large translations and rotations of the follicle in the skin when a force is applied to the stiff, proximal portion of the whisker (Video 6).

claim: Translations and rotations were not observed during contacts at the more flexible, distal portion of the whisker.
source: Translations and rotations were not observed during contacts at the more flexible, distal portion of the whisker
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Generalized linear models (GLMs) were employed to determine the relative importance of kinematic and mechanical variables in predicting neural firing.
source: We employed generalized linear models (GLMs) to determine the relative importance of kinematic and mechanical variables in predicting neural firing.

source: GLMs include linear combinations of the history of various input variables, as well as the non-linear characteristic of biological neurons, to predict the firing rate of a neuron given previously observed stimulus inputs and the resultant spiking patterns (Pillow et al., 2008).

claim: The GLM approach lends itself to the analysis of both active and passive deflections.
source: The GLM approach lends itself to the analysis of both active and passive deflections.

source: We invoke a formulation of the GLM in which the predictors are convolved with a set of nonlinear basis functions ('raised cosine bumps') that cover a desired temporal window into the past over which to consider the stimulus history (Pillow et al., 2008).

claim: A five dimensional basis was chosen for the GLM.
source: Here, we choose the five dimensional basis shown in Figure 4A.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: The basis functions extended 75 ms into the past, to match the temporal extent of the cross-correlations between the observed spikes and the various predictors while not being longer than the shortest inter-stimulus interval.
source: The basis functions extended 75 ms into the past, to match the temporal extent of the cross-correlations between the observed spikes and the various predictors while not being longer than the shortest inter-stimulus interval.

claim: The most recent time period is clearly the most important in predicting spikes for all six predictors.
source: The most recent time period is clearly the most important in predicting spikes for all six predictors.

claim: The very small values of the coefficients β5 associated with the basis function b5 indicate that there is no need to look much further than 25 ms into the past.
source: The very small values of the coefficients β5 associated with the basis function b5 indicate that there is no need to look much further than 25 ms into the past.

claim: Among all predictors, moment M has the largest coefficient β for the first four basis functions.
source: Among all predictors, moment M has the largest coefficient β for the first four basis functions

claim: On average, moment is the most important predictor of firing activity.

claim: Bending moment is not only the most important input to the example neuron in Figure 4C, but also emerges as the most important input across all neurons in Figure 4B.
source: Bending moment is not only the most important input to the example neuron in Figure 4C, but also emerges as the most important input across all neurons in Figure 4B.

claim: All input variables contribute to the GLM fits.

source: For neuron 24, the predictions of the mechanical subset model correspond well to those of the full model (R2 = 0.88), while the predictions of the kinematic subset model do not (R2 = 0.08).

source: This result indicates that the information present in the mechanical variables accounts for most of the information that the full model uses to predict spike rates.

source: An inverse relationship is apparent, indicating that if the predictions of one subset model account well for the predictions of the full model, the predictions of the other subset model do not.

claim: The median R value across all neurons for the full model is 0.30.
source: The median R value across all neurons is 0.30.

claim: There was no significant difference in full model performance between active contact and passive deflections (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p=0.18).
source: There was no significant difference between active contact and passive deflections (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p=0.18).

source: For the manual stimulation data, the median percent error for the mechanical subset models tend to lie closer to zero than the median percent error for the kinematic models (Wilcoxon signed rank test p<0.05)
